quiz.q: A 68-year-old on warfarin strikes his head getting out of a car. GCS 15, no vomiting, no amnesia, normal neurologic exam. What does the Canadian CT head rule contribute?
choices: It clears him from needing imaging
It applies and places him at medium risk only
Nothing, because anticoagulated patients are excluded from the rule and are imaged regardless
It requires a 2-hour observation before it can be applied
quiz.why: Anticoagulation, bleeding disorders and post-traumatic seizure are exclusion criteria, so the rule was never validated to clear those patients. Age 65 or older is also a high-risk criterion, but the exclusion settles the question first.

quiz.q: A 32-year-old restrained driver in a 25 mph collision is alert, sober, has no chest pain, no chest wall tenderness and no distracting injury. What does NEXUS Chest support?
choices: A chest CT to exclude aortic injury
No chest radiograph is required
A chest radiograph is required because of the mechanism
The rule cannot be applied under age 60
quiz.why: All seven NEXUS Chest criteria are negative, which supports omitting the film. A 25 mph collision does not meet the rapid deceleration threshold, and the rule applies across adult ages rather than only to those over 60.

quiz.q: A 71-year-old with a history of heart failure had syncope while gardening. Systolic pressure at triage was 86, the troponin is raised, and the emergency diagnosis is possible cardiac syncope. Roughly where does the Canadian Syncope Risk Score place him?
choices: Very low risk, suitable for discharge
Low risk, needing only follow-up
Medium risk with a serious event rate near 1 percent
High or very high risk, with a 30-day serious event rate above 20 percent
quiz.why: Heart disease 1, systolic pressure under 90 worth 2, raised troponin worth 2, and a cardiac syncope diagnosis worth 2 total at least 7. Scores of 4 and above exceed a 20 percent 30-day serious event rate.

quiz.q: Why has the San Francisco Syncope Rule fallen out of routine use despite excellent derivation performance?
choices: Its criteria require echocardiography
External validation produced widely varying sensitivity, from the 70s to the high 90s
It was replaced by a rule with fewer criteria
It only applies to patients over 65
quiz.why: Derivation studies routinely outperform validation studies, and this rule is the standard illustration. A rule is only trustworthy in a population resembling the validation cohort, which is the general caution that applies to every score.

quiz.q: A 64-year-old had 20 minutes of right arm weakness and slurred speech that fully resolved. Blood pressure is 152/88 and she has diabetes. What is her ABCD2 score and what should follow?
choices: Score 6, which by itself mandates thrombolysis
Score 4, but rapid vascular imaging and antiplatelet decisions are made regardless of the score
Score 2, which permits routine outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks
Score 7, the maximum, requiring intensive care admission
quiz.why: Age under 60 scores 0, blood pressure 1, unilateral weakness 2, duration 10 to 59 minutes 1, diabetes 1, for 5 by weakness or 4 depending on how speech is counted. Either way, a moderate score does not decide disposition, because a low score does not exclude critical carotid stenosis.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old man has migrating right lower quadrant pain, anorexia, nausea, focal tenderness with rebound, a temperature of 37.6 C, a white count of 14,000 and 80 percent neutrophils. What is his Alvarado score and what does it support?
choices: Score 4, meaning appendicitis is unlikely
Score 6, meaning discharge with return precautions
Score 10, meaning appendicitis is likely and surgery should be involved
Score 7, but the score is invalid in male patients
quiz.why: Migration 1, anorexia 1, nausea 1, tenderness 2, rebound 1, temperature 1, leukocytosis 2, left shift 1 totals 10. Scores of 7 to 10 support appendicitis and warrant a surgical conversation alongside imaging.

quiz.q: A patient with acute pancreatitis is being triaged 90 minutes after arrival. Why does the Ranson score not help this decision?
choices: It requires a CT scan that has not been done
Six of its eleven criteria are measured at 48 hours, so the score cannot be completed yet
It only applies to gallstone pancreatitis
It has been withdrawn from use
quiz.why: Ranson is a prognostic score that becomes complete only at 48 hours, which makes it useless for a first-hour decision. Recognizing the difference between a prognostic score and a triage tool applies to a whole family of scores.

quiz.q: A 40-year-old with one episode of melena has a normal blood pressure, a pulse of 78, hemoglobin 15.1, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, no syncope, no liver disease and no heart failure. Which score and result is relevant?
choices: A Rockall score, which requires endoscopy first
A CURB-65 score of 0
A Glasgow-Blatchford score suggesting he may be manageable as an outpatient
A HAS-BLED score of 0
quiz.why: Glasgow-Blatchford uses only pre-endoscopic data and is specifically designed to identify upper gastrointestinal bleeds safe for outpatient management. Rockall requires endoscopic findings, and the other scores answer entirely different questions.

quiz.q: Which statement comparing PSI and CURB-65 for pneumonia is most accurate?
choices: PSI uses about 20 variables and is better at confirming low risk, while CURB-65 is faster at the bedside
CURB-65 is more accurate but requires arterial blood gas sampling
PSI and CURB-65 use identical variables with different weighting
PSI applies only to patients over 65
quiz.why: PSI spans about 20 demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory and imaging variables across five classes and identifies the genuinely low-risk patient confidently. CURB-65 trades some accuracy for being calculable in half a minute.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has hypertension, diabetes and prior vascular disease. What is her CHA2DS2-VASc score and what follows?
choices: Score 3, no anticoagulation needed in women
Score 2, monitor only
Score 6, refer for ablation instead of anticoagulation
Score 5, which is above the threshold, so anticoagulation is indicated
quiz.why: Hypertension 1, diabetes 1, vascular disease 1, age 65 to 74 worth 1, and female sex 1 total 5. The threshold is 3 or more in women, so she is well above it and anticoagulation is indicated.

quiz.q: A patient with atrial fibrillation has a HAS-BLED score of 4, largely from uncontrolled hypertension, daily NSAID use, and heavy alcohol intake. What does this correctly trigger?
choices: Withholding anticoagulation and using aspirin instead
Correcting the modifiable items and following the patient more closely, while still anticoagulating
Permanent avoidance of all antithrombotic therapy
An immediate referral for left atrial appendage occlusion as the only option
quiz.why: Every item driving this score is modifiable. HAS-BLED was built to identify correctable risks and patients needing closer follow-up, not to veto anticoagulation, and aspirin is inferior for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the GRACE score from the TIMI score in acute coronary syndromes?
choices: GRACE uses continuous variables and predicts mortality, with scores above 140 supporting an early invasive strategy
GRACE uses fewer variables and is faster to calculate
TIMI predicts mortality while GRACE predicts bleeding
TIMI requires echocardiographic data
quiz.why: TIMI is seven yes-or-no items predicting a composite event rate. GRACE incorporates continuous variables including age, heart rate, pressure, creatinine and Killip class to predict mortality, and a score above 140 identifies patients benefiting from catheterization within 24 hours.

quiz.q: A 52-year-old describes chest pain that reached maximum intensity instantly and radiates between his shoulder blades. Which question best moves the differential?
choices: How severe is the pain on a scale of 1 to 10?
Does it hurt more when you press on your chest?
Did the pain peak instantly or build over minutes, and is there a difference between your arms?
Have you eaten anything unusual today?
quiz.why: Instantaneous maximal onset with interscapular radiation raises aortic dissection, and comparing arm pressures is the bedside maneuver that follows. Severity does not separate diagnoses, and chest wall tenderness fails to exclude either dissection or coronary occlusion.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old with atrial fibrillation has 10 out of 10 abdominal pain and a soft, minimally tender abdomen with normal initial laboratory values. What does this pattern indicate?
choices: Mesenteric ischemia, where early findings are unimpressive because the bowel wall has not yet become inflamed
Constipation with anxiety
Gastroenteritis in the prodromal phase
Renal colic radiating anteriorly
quiz.why: Pain out of proportion to the examination in a patient with an embolic source is mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise. Normal early laboratory values are expected and are one of the reasons the diagnosis is missed.

quiz.q: A 60-year-old reports dizziness. Which finding most strongly suggests a central rather than a peripheral cause?
choices: Nausea with the episodes
Symptoms worsening when rolling over in bed
A sensation of the room spinning
Inability to stand and walk without assistance
quiz.why: Benign positional vertigo is miserable but patients remain ambulatory. Inability to walk unaided is one of the strongest discriminators for a central lesion. Nausea, spinning and positional worsening all occur in peripheral causes.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old collapsed while playing basketball, with no warning symptoms beforehand. His uncle died suddenly at 35. What is the most important implication?
choices: This is likely vasovagal syncope from exertion and dehydration
Exertional syncope with a family history of sudden death points at structural or electrical cardiac disease
Orthostatic hypotension from inadequate fluid intake
A simple faint that needs only observation and discharge
quiz.why: Vasovagal syncope typically has a prodrome and occurs at rest or on standing, not at peak exertion. Syncope during exertion plus a family history of sudden death raises hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, anomalous coronaries, and inherited arrhythmia syndromes.

quiz.q: A 44-year-old has one swollen, painful leg that became tense over 6 hours with pain far exceeding the visible findings. What must be considered beyond deep vein thrombosis?
choices: Venous insufficiency and dependent edema
A ruptured Baker cyst
Necrotizing soft tissue infection and compartment syndrome
Lymphedema
quiz.why: Rapid onset with pain out of proportion is the shared signature of necrotizing infection and compartment syndrome, both of which are limb-threatening and both of which look unremarkable early. Venous insufficiency and lymphedema develop slowly and are usually bilateral.

quiz.q: Which pair of bedside tests changes more differentials than any imaging study?
choices: Glucose and pregnancy test
Lactate and procalcitonin
D-dimer and troponin
Urinalysis and complete blood count
quiz.why: Hypoglycemia imitates stroke, seizure, intoxication and psychosis and is reversible in minutes. Pregnancy changes the differential and the imaging choices for every abdominal and pelvic complaint in half the population.

quiz.q: A 38-year-old with a sore throat cannot swallow his saliva, has a muffled voice and sits leaning forward. What is the priority?
choices: A rapid streptococcal test and antibiotics
Anticipating an airway emergency and getting senior help before any throat examination
Ibuprofen and discharge with fluids
A monospot test for infectious mononucleosis
quiz.why: Drooling, a muffled voice and tripod posture indicate supraglottic swelling that can close the airway. Examining the throat may precipitate obstruction, so the priority is preparation and experienced help, not a swab.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old presents with vomiting alone, no abdominal pain and no diarrhea. Which must-not-miss diagnosis is most frequently overlooked in this presentation?
choices: Norovirus infection
Myocardial infarction presenting atypically
Gastroesophageal reflux disease
Motion sickness
quiz.why: In older patients, women and those with diabetes, an infarct can present as nausea and vomiting with no chest pain at all. Obstruction and raised intracranial pressure are the other two dangerous causes of isolated vomiting.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old has a fever and a purple spotted rash on the shins that does not blanch under glass pressure. What does this combination mean?
choices: Drug eruption, needing antihistamines
Blood outside the vessels, meaning meningococcemia until proven otherwise
Urticaria from a food allergy
A viral exanthem needing supportive care only
quiz.why: Blanching indicates dilated vessels with intact walls, which covers most rashes. A non-blanching rash means extravasated blood, and combined with fever in a young adult that is meningococcal sepsis until antibiotics and cultures prove otherwise.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old started an antibiotic 10 days ago and now has a painful rash with erosions inside the mouth and crusting on the lips. What does the mucosal involvement indicate?
choices: A benign drug rash that will resolve on stopping the drug
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which is a dermatologic emergency
Primary herpes simplex infection
quiz.why: Mucosal involvement of the mouth, eyes or genitals within about three weeks of a new drug separates Stevens-Johnson syndrome from an ordinary drug eruption. It carries significant mortality and requires urgent specialist involvement.

quiz.q: A 62-year-old man with known gout has a single hot, swollen, exquisitely painful knee and a temperature of 38.1 C. What is the correct approach?
choices: Treat as a gout flare, since he has a documented history
Start colchicine and arrange rheumatology follow-up
Apply ice and immobilize, with reassessment in 48 hours
Arrange joint aspiration, because this is septic arthritis until proven otherwise
quiz.why: A known crystal arthropathy does not protect against infection, and the two can coexist in the same joint. Only synovial fluid analysis with Gram stain, culture and crystal examination separates them, and a missed septic joint destroys cartilage within days.

quiz.q: A 17-year-old has had severe left scrotal pain for 9 hours with vomiting, and reports two similar episodes in the past month that resolved on their own. How should the prior episodes be interpreted?
choices: As reassurance, since previous episodes resolved without harm
As evidence of chronic epididymitis
As a warning sign of intermittent torsion, which makes this episode more concerning rather than less
As irrelevant to the current presentation
quiz.why: Intermittent torsion with spontaneous detorsion produces exactly this history and identifies a testicle that is anatomically prone to twisting. Salvage falls sharply after 12 hours, so the prior episodes add urgency rather than reassurance.

quiz.q: Which one-liner is constructed correctly for a patient presentation?
choices: Room 8, chest pain, needs a monitor
67-year-old woman with COPD and heart failure, here with three days of worsening shortness of breath and leg swelling
A pleasant elderly lady who is a poor historian, possible pneumonia versus heart failure versus COPD
67-year-old woman, tonsillectomy 1968, two children, retired teacher, here today feeling unwell
quiz.why: The one-liner carries age, sex, the history that matters for this encounter, the complaint and the duration, and nothing else. Room numbers, unrelated history and a list of hypotheses all fail to load the right illness scripts.

quiz.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has a potassium of 5.4 mEq/L. Why does this delay insulin rather than reassure?
choices: Because insulin raises potassium and risks hyperkalemia
Because acidosis shifts potassium out of cells, so the serum value hides a total-body deficit that insulin will unmask
Because potassium above 5.0 is a contraindication to fluids
Because the potassium must be corrected to normal before any treatment begins
quiz.why: Acidosis and insulin deficiency drive potassium out of cells, so a normal or high serum level coexists with a large whole-body deficit. Insulin drives it back in, and giving insulin to a patient whose potassium is already low can precipitate arrhythmia.

quiz.q: A presentation of a thunderclap headache ends with the assessment. What would improve it most?
choices: Adding a longer past medical history
Listing every negative review of systems item
Ending with a specific request, such as asking for the CT to be ordered now given the 6-hour window
Adding the patient's insurance status
quiz.why: A presentation that ends without a request leaves the listener guessing what is wanted. Naming the specific next action, and the reason timing matters, converts a report into a decision the listener can approve or redirect.

quiz.q: An 81-year-old on apixaban falls, strikes his head, and has a GCS of 15 with a normal exam. Beyond imaging, what is the second question the assessment should address?
choices: Why he fell, since a medication or orthostatic cause changes the disposition
Whether he has had a tetanus vaccination
Whether the fall was witnessed by more than one person
Whether he prefers a private room
quiz.why: A fall is an event with a cause, and in an older patient on multiple medications the cause is frequently orthostatic hypotension, a new drug, arrhythmia, or infection. Treating the head injury without answering why he fell guarantees the next fall.

quiz.q: In a 67-year-old with both COPD and heart failure, which cluster of findings best supports heart failure as the current driver?
choices: Diffuse wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, and a smoking history
Fever, productive sputum, and a focal infiltrate
Orthostatic dizziness, dry mucous membranes, and a soft blood pressure
Orthopnea at three pillows, 6 lb weight gain, jugular venous distention, and a BNP of 780
quiz.why: Orthopnea, weight gain, distended neck veins and a raised BNP are volume findings that COPD does not produce. Wheeze occurs in both conditions, and fever with a focal infiltrate would point at pneumonia instead.

quiz.q: A discharge note for mechanical low back pain lists every red flag as specifically screened and absent. What does this accomplish?
choices: It satisfies a billing requirement only
It proves the differential was actually run, which is what makes a benign diagnosis defensible
It replaces the need for return precautions
It substitutes for imaging
quiz.why: A benign diagnosis is only credible if the record shows the dangerous ones were considered. Documented pertinent negatives are that evidence, and they remain necessary alongside, not instead of, specific return precautions.

quiz.q: Which entry belongs in the assessment rather than the objective section of a note?
choices: Acute decompensated heart failure with secondary bronchospasm
BNP 780 pg/mL
Bilateral pitting edema to mid-shin
Respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air
quiz.why: The objective section holds measurements and observations without interpretation. Edema, a laboratory value and vital signs are findings; the diagnosis that explains all of them is the assessment.

quiz.q: Which set of return precautions is written correctly for a patient discharged with back pain?
choices: Return if your symptoms do not improve
Follow up with your doctor as needed
Return immediately for numbness in the groin or inner thighs, trouble starting or controlling urination, new leg weakness, fever, or pain that wakes you at night
Return if you feel that something is wrong
quiz.why: Return precautions must name the specific findings that correspond to the diagnoses the workup could not exclude, in this case cauda equina, infection and malignancy. Generic instructions give the patient nothing actionable.

quiz.q: A plan section reads: non-contrast head CT now. What single addition would most improve it?
choices: The estimated radiation dose
What happens if the CT is negative, such as lumbar puncture versus CT angiography
The name of the radiology technologist
The patient's preferred pharmacy
quiz.why: A plan that stops at the first order leaves the next clinician without the reasoning. Stating the decision point, and what each result triggers, is what makes the plan transferable across a shift change.

quiz.q: Which part of an abstract should be read first?
choices: The conclusion, since it summarizes the finding
The population enrolled and excluded
The funding disclosure
The statistical methods
quiz.why: Who was studied determines whether the result applies to your patient at all, and exclusion criteria often remove exactly the patients you see. The conclusion is the authors' interpretation and is read last, after the absolute numbers.

quiz.q: A trial reports a 45 percent relative reduction in a composite of death, reinfarction and unplanned revascularization. What is the most important next question?
choices: Which component drove the result, and what was the absolute risk reduction
Which journal published it
How many authors were listed
Whether the trial was conducted internationally
quiz.why: Composite endpoints are commonly driven by their softest component, here revascularization, which is partly a clinician decision. A relative figure without an absolute one also conceals how small the real benefit may be.

quiz.q: A test with 95 percent sensitivity and 45 percent specificity is used in 1,000 patients with a 10 percent disease prevalence. How many false negatives occur?
choices: About 495
About 405
About 5
About 95
quiz.why: One hundred patients have the disease and 95 percent sensitivity catches 95 of them, leaving 5 false negatives. The 495 figure is false positives, and 405 is true negatives.

quiz.q: The same 95 percent sensitive, 45 percent specific test is applied where prevalence is 40 percent. The negative predictive value falls to about 93 percent. What does that mean for practice?
choices: The test has become less sensitive in sicker patients
A negative result now leaves roughly 7 percent residual risk, which is too high to end the workup
The test should be repeated to improve accuracy
Specificity must be recalculated for this population
quiz.why: Sensitivity and specificity did not change; only the population did. At 7 percent residual risk a negative result no longer clears the patient, which is precisely why pretest probability must be estimated before ordering.

quiz.q: A therapy reduces an outcome from 12 percent to 9 percent over 3 years. What are the absolute risk reduction and the number needed to treat?
choices: 3 percent and an NNT of about 33 over 3 years
25 percent and an NNT of 4
3 percent and an NNT of 3
9 percent and an NNT of 11
quiz.why: Absolute risk reduction is 12 minus 9, which is 3 percentage points, and NNT is 1 divided by 0.03, about 33. The 25 percent figure is the relative risk reduction, which describes the same data more flatteringly.

quiz.q: A colleague quotes an NNT of 20 for a medication without further detail. What is missing?
choices: The manufacturer's name
The time frame and the population it applies to
The cost per dose
The route of administration
quiz.why: An NNT is meaningless without over what period and in which patients. An NNT of 20 over 5 years in high-risk secondary prevention is a different claim from an NNT of 20 over 30 days in a general population.

quiz.q: Why does per-protocol analysis flatter a treatment compared with intention-to-treat?
choices: It includes more patients and therefore has more statistical power
It analyzes only patients who completed the treatment, removing those who could not tolerate or adhere to it
It uses a longer follow-up period
It compares against a weaker placebo
quiz.why: Dropping the patients who stopped the drug removes exactly the people in whom it failed or caused harm, leaving a selected group who did well. Intention-to-treat keeps everyone in the group they were assigned to, which mirrors real practice.

quiz.q: An intoxicated patient who struck his head is arousable, states the risk of a brain bleed back to you, weighs it against wanting to go home, and gives the same answer each time. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: He lacks capacity because his blood alcohol level is elevated
He demonstrates capacity for this decision and may refuse, with documentation of the assessment
A court order is required before he can refuse
Only a psychiatrist can make this determination
quiz.why: Capacity is decision-specific and assessed clinically through understanding, appreciation, reasoning and a consistent choice. A blood alcohol level measures a substance, not decision-making, and competence is the separate legal status decided by a court.

quiz.q: A 16-year-old requests testing for a sexually transmitted infection and asks that her parents not be told. What is the correct approach?
choices: Refuse until a parent consents in all circumstances
Promise complete confidentiality immediately to build trust
Check the state's specific minor consent provisions and be honest about what billing and portal notifications may disclose
Treat her as emancipated because she came in alone
quiz.why: Most states permit minors to consent independently for sexually transmitted infection care, but categories and ages vary and must be verified locally. Promising confidentiality without checking how the visit is billed and posted is a promise that cannot be kept.

quiz.q: A capacitated adult with a hemoglobin of 5.8 refuses transfusion on religious grounds. What does appropriate care look like?
choices: Transfuse anyway once she becomes hypotensive, since the emergency exception applies
Honor the refusal and treat aggressively with everything she does accept, such as iron, tranexamic acid, endoscopic control and cell salvage
Discharge her, since she is refusing treatment
Ask the family to override her decision
quiz.why: A capacitated adult may refuse any treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, and refusing one therapy is not refusing care. The emergency exception applies only when a patient cannot consent, and a family cannot override a capacitated patient.

quiz.q: A caller states he is a patient's brother and asks for her test results. What is the correct response?
choices: Provide the results, since family members are permitted access
Provide only the abnormal results
Ask for his date of birth to verify identity and then provide the results
Decline to release information, because identity cannot be verified by telephone and authorization has not been established
quiz.why: Telephone identity cannot be verified and being a relative does not by itself create a right to the information. Authorization comes from the patient, and the safe answer is to take a message or route the caller rather than release anything.

quiz.q: An 84-year-old with metastatic cancer and a valid POLST specifying comfort care arrives in respiratory distress. Her son demands intubation. What should happen?
choices: Honor the POLST, and handle the son's demand as grief needing information about what comfort care actively includes
Intubate, since a family member present outranks a document
Intubate briefly and extubate once the son calms down
Call security to remove the son from the department
quiz.why: A valid POLST records the patient's own expressed wishes and takes precedence over a surrogate's preference. Comfort care is an active plan with oxygen, opioids for dyspnea, antiemetics, positioning and presence, and saying so is what usually resolves the conflict.

quiz.q: A patient with epigastric burning improves after an antacid and is nearly discharged before an ECG shows an inferior STEMI. Which pair of biases best explains this?
choices: Availability and diagnosis momentum
Attribution bias and confirmation bias
Anchoring on the initial label, followed by premature closure when the antacid appeared to help
Base rate neglect and hindsight bias
quiz.why: The first label fixed the frame, and the apparent treatment response ended the search. A therapeutic response is not a diagnostic test, because cardiac pain responds to antacids often enough that the improvement carries little discriminating value.

quiz.q: A department has admitted three influenza cases this shift. The fourth febrile patient with body aches is swabbed and discharged, and returns in septic shock from a spinal epidural abscess; back pain was documented at the first visit. Which two failures occurred?
choices: Diagnosis momentum and attribution bias
Base rate neglect and anchoring
Confirmation bias and hindsight bias
Availability bias and search satisficing, since the back pain was never explained
quiz.why: Recent vivid cases made influenza feel most likely, and the search stopped at the first plausible fit. The unexplained back pain was the finding that did not fit, and asking whether the diagnosis explains every finding is the habit that catches it.

scenarios.title: Syncope: which rule, and what it actually says
scenarios.intro: A 68-year-old man is brought in after collapsing in a supermarket aisle. Witnesses say he was standing still, went pale and slumped, and was out for maybe fifteen seconds with no shaking. He has hypertension and a remote myocardial infarction. You are going to reason through this the way the provider will, one decision at a time.

steps.prompt: He is awake and back to baseline, and tells you he felt nothing beforehand. No warmth, no nausea, no tunnel vision, no lightheadedness. He was just standing there, and then he was on the floor with people around him.

choices.text: Record the absence of a prodrome as a significant finding and get a 12-lead ECG immediately
choices.feedback: Correct. Vasovagal syncope almost always has a warning: warmth, nausea, greying vision, sweating. Collapse with no prodrome at all, in an older patient with prior infarction, shifts probability toward an arrhythmia, and the ECG is the first test in every syncope workup.

choices.text: Record it as an uncomplicated faint, since he recovered fully and quickly
choices.feedback: Rapid full recovery is typical of arrhythmic syncope too, because once the rhythm resolves so does the perfusion. Recovery speed does not separate benign from dangerous causes.

choices.text: Focus the history on whether he had eaten and how hot the store was
choices.feedback: Situational triggers matter, but chasing them first risks building a benign story before the dangerous ones are addressed. Ask about them after the prodrome question and the ECG.

steps.prompt: The ECG shows sinus bradycardia at `56`, a QRS of `136 ms`, a QTc of `492 ms`, and an axis of `-45` degrees. The initial troponin is at the upper limit of normal, and a repeat is pending. He has no chest pain and no shortness of breath.

choices.text: Score the Canadian Syncope Risk Score, since these ECG findings are exactly what it weighs
choices.feedback: Correct. Heart disease, abnormal axis, QRS over 130 ms and QTc over 480 ms are all scored items. The rule exists because these individually modest abnormalities add up to a risk estimate a gut impression tends to underrate.

choices.text: Apply the San Francisco rule, since the ECG is abnormal, and stop there
choices.feedback: The rule would flag him, which is not wrong, but its validation performance varied widely and it gives a binary answer rather than a graded risk. It is the weaker of the two tools here.

choices.text: Treat the findings as chronic and unrelated, since he has no cardiac symptoms today
choices.feedback: Absence of chest pain does not make a conduction abnormality irrelevant to a syncopal event. Conduction disease is the mechanism by which a patient with no symptoms collapses without warning.

steps.prompt: You total the score: history of heart disease `+1`, abnormal QRS axis `+1`, QRS over `130 ms` `+1`, QTc over `480 ms` `+2`. No vasovagal predisposition to subtract, and the emergency diagnosis is not vasovagal. The total is `5`.

choices.text: Recognize this as high risk, above a 20 percent chance of a serious 30-day event, and argue for monitored admission
choices.feedback: Correct. Scores of 4 and above carry a serious adverse event rate above 20 percent within 30 days. That is the number that turns a well-appearing man who feels fine into an admission.

choices.text: Treat 5 as medium risk and arrange outpatient cardiac monitoring in a week
choices.feedback: Medium risk is roughly 1 to 3 on this score. Five sits in the high band, and a week of unmonitored time is exactly the window the score is warning about.

choices.text: Note the score but defer entirely to the attending's gestalt
choices.feedback: Gestalt and score should be reconciled out loud, not one silently discarded. If the attending disagrees, the reason belongs in the note.

steps.prompt: The attending agrees with admission. She asks you what you would have done differently if the same man had described feeling hot, nauseated and greyed-out for `20` seconds before collapsing while donating blood, with a completely normal ECG.

choices.text: Score it again: vasovagal predisposition minus 1, vasovagal diagnosis minus 2, no ECG points, giving a very low score and supporting discharge
choices.feedback: Correct. Those two negative items exist precisely to let a clear vasovagal story pull the score down. A very low score carries a serious event rate near 0.4 percent, which supports discharge with follow-up.

choices.text: Admit anyway, because all syncope in a patient over 65 requires admission
choices.feedback: Age alone is not the deciding variable, and admitting every older syncope patient is neither feasible nor supported. The score exists to separate them.

choices.text: Discharge without scoring, since a classic vasovagal story speaks for itself
choices.feedback: The story does most of the work, and scoring it anyway takes thirty seconds and documents the reasoning. The point of a rule is that the decision becomes defensible in writing.

scenarios.debrief: Two patients, both older, both briefly unconscious, both fine on arrival. The difference is entirely in the history and the ECG, and the rule is what turns those details into a number that can be acted on and written down. The single most useful history question in syncope is whether there was a prodrome, because vasovagal syncope warns and arrhythmic syncope usually does not. The second most useful is whether it happened during exertion. The Canadian Syncope Risk Score weighs nine items, and its two negative items exist so a convincing benign story can lower the score rather than just failing to raise it. What the case really teaches is the general principle behind every decision rule: individually modest abnormalities, a slightly wide QRS, a slightly long QTc, an abnormal axis, add up to a risk that clinical impression consistently underestimates. That is what a rule is for, and it is also why an override, in either direction, is written down with its reason.

scenarios.title: Right lower quadrant pain in a 24-year-old woman
scenarios.intro: A 24-year-old woman arrives with abdominal pain that started around her navel yesterday evening and has settled into the right lower quadrant. She has no medical history and takes no medications. She is uncomfortable but walking. You are the technician assigned to her, and the provider is tied up in a resuscitation for the next fifteen minutes.

steps.prompt: You are getting her on the monitor and taking vitals. She tells you the pain is `7` out of `10`, constant, worse when the stretcher moves, and that she has not wanted to eat since last night.

choices.text: Ask when her last menstrual period was, and make sure a urine pregnancy test is collected
choices.feedback: Correct. Ectopic pregnancy is the must-not-miss in a woman of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain, and the result changes both the differential and which imaging is appropriate. Collecting the specimen early saves twenty minutes later.

choices.text: Ask about recent travel and food, since gastroenteritis is common at her age
choices.feedback: Reasonable history, wrong priority. Migration from periumbilical to right lower quadrant with anorexia is not a gastroenteritis pattern, and the pregnancy question comes first regardless.

choices.text: Wait for the provider before asking any history questions
choices.feedback: Asking onset, migration, last menstrual period and appetite while placing a line is not stepping outside a technician's role. Those answers are exactly what the provider will want in the first thirty seconds.

steps.prompt: Her last period was three weeks ago and the pregnancy test is negative. The provider arrives and examines her: focal tenderness in the right lower quadrant with voluntary guarding, no rigidity, no rebound elicited. The white count returns at `13,200` with `82%` neutrophils.

choices.text: Total the Alvarado score and recognize it is in the imaging band, not the discharge band
choices.feedback: Correct. Migration 1, anorexia 1, nausea 1, tenderness 2, temperature 1, leukocytosis 2, left shift 1 comes to 9 without rebound. Scores of 7 and above support appendicitis and a surgical conversation alongside imaging.

choices.text: Conclude appendicitis is unlikely because rebound tenderness is absent
choices.feedback: Rebound is one point out of ten and is frequently absent early, before the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum. Its absence does not lower probability meaningfully.

choices.text: Suggest discharge with a recheck in 12 hours since she is well appearing
choices.feedback: Well appearing is compatible with early appendicitis, which is exactly the stage where perforation is preventable. A score in this range earns imaging today.

steps.prompt: The provider is writing the imaging order and thinking out loud. She says the Alvarado score is high and appendicitis leads, but she wants to name the competing diagnosis before she commits.

choices.text: Ovarian torsion, because the score loses specificity in women of childbearing age and imaging should assess the adnexa
choices.feedback: Correct. Torsion, tubo-ovarian abscess and ruptured cysts all generate Alvarado points, which is why the score performs worst in exactly this population. Naming it changes what the imaging must answer.

choices.text: Renal colic, because right lower quadrant pain can be ureteric
choices.feedback: Worth considering and it fits poorly here. Renal colic is classically colicky and makes patients restless rather than still, and it does not produce migration from the periumbilical region with anorexia.

choices.text: Nothing else is needed, since the score is high enough to be definitive
choices.feedback: A score supports a decision, it does not close a differential. Premature closure after a high score is the same error as premature closure after a treatment response.

steps.prompt: Imaging confirms acute appendicitis with no adnexal abnormality. Surgery is consulted. The provider asks you to summarize the case to the surgical resident who is on the way down.

choices.text: Give the one-liner, the migration history, the Alvarado score, the negative pregnancy test, the imaging result, and say surgery has been consulted
choices.feedback: Correct. One-liner, the evidence in the order it was gathered, the exclusions, the result, and where things stand. A consultant wants the reason for the call near the front and the specifics behind it.

choices.text: Say the CT showed appendicitis and leave it there
choices.feedback: True and incomplete. The surgeon needs the duration, the pregnancy status and the examination, because those change the urgency and the operative plan.

choices.text: Read the chart from the beginning, starting with her arrival time and registration details
choices.feedback: Presenting front to back forces the listener to assemble the picture themselves. The structure exists because a listener builds a diagnosis in a particular order.

scenarios.debrief: The case is deliberately straightforward so the reasoning is visible. Three things happened that would not have happened automatically. First, the pregnancy question was asked in the first two minutes by whoever was in the room, because ectopic pregnancy is the must-not-miss and the answer redirects everything. Second, a decision rule was totaled rather than eyeballed, which moved a well-appearing patient into the imaging band. Third, and most important, the competing diagnosis was named out loud before the imaging was ordered, which is what made the study answer two questions instead of one. Alvarado performs worst in women of childbearing age precisely because gynecologic disease generates the same points, so a high score in this population is a reason to image the adnexa, not a reason to stop thinking. The pattern to carry: a score that supports your leading diagnosis is the moment you are most likely to close prematurely.

scenarios.title: He wants to leave, and the question is capacity
scenarios.intro: A 52-year-old man was brought in by ambulance after a witnessed fall down four concrete steps outside a bar. He smells strongly of alcohol, has an abrasion over the right temple, and has been in the department for forty minutes. He is now sitting up, pulling at the monitor leads, and saying he is going home. The provider asks you to help work through whether he can.

steps.prompt: He is awake, speaking in full sentences, mildly slurred. He says his head is fine, he just wants his shoes. He is oriented to place and roughly to time, and can tell you what happened.

choices.text: Begin a structured capacity assessment: can he understand, appreciate, reason, and express a consistent choice
choices.feedback: Correct. Capacity is decision-specific and assessed now, at this moment, for this decision. The four components are the assessment, and running them in order is what makes the answer defensible either way.

choices.text: Tell him he cannot leave because he is intoxicated
choices.feedback: Intoxication does not automatically remove capacity, and asserting that it does without an assessment is both clinically and legally weak. Some intoxicated patients retain capacity and some do not.

choices.text: Call security to keep him in the room while someone finds the attending
choices.feedback: Restraint of any kind requires a determination that he lacks capacity and is at risk. Starting with force rather than assessment escalates a situation that may not need it.

steps.prompt: You explain the concern. He repeats it back: "You think I could have bleeding in my head from hitting it, and you want a scan." Asked what could happen if he leaves, he says, "I could have a bleed and not know, and I could get worse at home." Asked why he still wants to go, he says his dog has been alone since noon and he lives alone.

choices.text: Note that he has demonstrated understanding, appreciation and reasoning, and test whether the choice is consistent when re-asked
choices.feedback: Correct. He has met three of the four components explicitly. Consistency over time is the fourth, and it is the one that most often fails in a patient whose mental status is changing.

choices.text: Conclude he lacks capacity because wanting to go home to a dog is not a rational reason
choices.feedback: Capacity assesses the process, not whether the clinician agrees with the values. Weighing a real personal obligation against a medical risk is reasoning, even if you would weigh it differently.

choices.text: Conclude he has capacity and stop, since he said the right words once
choices.feedback: One correct answer is not a consistent choice, and an evolving head injury changes mental status over minutes. Re-asking is part of the assessment, not a formality.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes later you re-ask. This time he cannot recall why a scan was suggested, asks whether he is at work, and then says he wants to leave to catch a bus that does not run at this hour. His speech is more slurred than before.

choices.text: Report the change immediately: he no longer demonstrates capacity, and the deterioration itself is a clinical finding
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. The capacity assessment has changed and so has the neurologic picture. A patient becoming less oriented after a head strike is not sobering up, and that distinction is the entire case.

choices.text: Assume he is simply becoming more intoxicated as the alcohol absorbs, and let him sleep
choices.feedback: This is the reasoning that kills these patients. Alcohol levels fall over time in the department, so worsening mental status after arrival points at an intracranial process, not at alcohol.

choices.text: Repeat the capacity questions a third time before telling anyone
choices.feedback: The change is already documented across two assessments, and a declining GCS after head trauma is time-critical. Report first, reassess after.

steps.prompt: CT shows an acute subdural hematoma. Neurosurgery is called. His sister arrives and asks why he was not simply allowed to leave when he asked, since he seemed fine and it is his right.

choices.text: Explain that capacity was assessed, documented, and then changed, and that the change in his answers was itself the warning sign that led to the scan
choices.feedback: Correct. It is an honest account and it is also the clinical story. The serial assessment was not bureaucracy; it was the monitoring that caught the deterioration.

choices.text: Tell her he was never allowed to leave because intoxicated patients cannot refuse care
choices.feedback: This is inaccurate and undercuts the actual reasoning. Intoxicated patients can and sometimes do refuse care, which is exactly why the assessment was done rather than assumed.

choices.text: Say the decision was made by the attending and refer her onward without explanation
choices.feedback: Deflecting is safe but unhelpful. A plain factual account of what was assessed and what changed is both accurate and what she is actually asking for.

scenarios.debrief: Two things run in parallel here and they turn out to be the same thing. The first is the ethics question: capacity is decision-specific, assessed at this moment, and built from four components, understanding, appreciation, reasoning and a consistent choice. It is not determined by a blood alcohol level, and it is not determined by whether the clinician agrees with the patient's values. The second is the clinical question, and the serial capacity assessment happened to be the tool that answered it. A patient who becomes less oriented over forty minutes in an emergency department is not becoming more intoxicated, because alcohol levels fall with time. Worsening mental status after a head strike is an expanding intracranial process until imaging says otherwise. The general pattern: re-asking is not a formality. A capacity assessment that is repeated is also a neurologic examination that is repeated, and in a head-injured patient the trend is the finding.
